spans.note: Restates the hypothesis under test and describes the source dataset (146,028 dyads, four leagues, 2012-2013 season)

spans.assertion: the adjusted risk difference between dark-skinned and light-skinned players is 0.125 percentage points (95% CI: -0.088 to 0.337, p=0.249), a small non-significant increase
the hypothesis is not supported; the effect is not significant at α=0.05, the CI includes zero, and the null of no difference cannot be rejected
the primary estimand (adjusted risk difference) is estimated at 0.1247 percentage points, 95% CI (-0.0875, 0.3369), two-sided p=0.2493, SE=0.1083

dark-skinned players have a 0.125pp higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players after adjusting for games, position, and league country, but the difference is not statistically significant and the CI includes zero
the baseline red card rate for light-skinned players is 1.22%, so the 0.125pp increase is roughly a 10% relative increase with substantial uncertainty
the secondary estimand (adjusted odds ratio) is estimated at 1.110, 95% CI (0.929, 1.326), two-sided p=0.2493
dark-skinned players have 1.11 times the odds of a red card versus light-skinned players; the CI includes 1.0, so not significant

spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample Size subheading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis chosen was the player-referee dyad
the final analysis sample contains 109,337 dyads
the sample includes 1,372 unique players (263 dark-skinned, 1,109 light-skinned)
the sample includes 2,865 unique referees
1,356 dyads (1.24%) had at least one red card observed
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for whether any red card occurred in the dyad across all encounters
red cards are rare events, occurring in only 1.24% of dyads
skin tone exposure was sourced from averaging two independent raters' assessments of player profile photos
inter-rater reliability between the two raters' skin tone assessments was 0.923
the skin tone measure used a 0 to 1 scale (0=very light, 1=very dark)
light skin was defined as average rating ≤0.25 (89,611 dyads, 81.96%) and dark skin as average rating ≥0.50 (19,726 dyads, 18.04%)
the medium skin tone group (0.25-0.50), 14,598 dyads, was excluded from the primary analysis

spans.note: Lead-in stating the model adjusted for covariates listed below

spans.assertion: games (number of encounters between player and referee) was included as a continuous covariate, mean=3.0, SD=3.6
games has a strong positive association with red cards
player position was included as a categorical covariate with 8 groups (Goalkeeper, Center Back, Center Forward, Defensive Midfielder, Attacking Midfielder, Left Fullback, Right Fullback, Other)
Center Back has the highest red card rate among position groups
defensive players such as Center Backs receive red cards at nearly double the rate of attacking players
league country was included as a categorical covariate with 4 levels: England, France, Germany, Spain
France and Spain show higher red card rates than England, while Germany is similar to England

spans.note: Interpretive remark that league effects capture refereeing culture/enforcement differences

spans.assertion: 21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin tone ratings (no photo or rating)
14,598 dyads (11.7% of rated sample) with medium skin tone were excluded to create a clear light/dark contrast
686 dyads (0.6%) were excluded for missing height/weight data to allow complete case analysis
the total analysis sample is 109,337 dyads, 74.9% of the original dataset
missingness in photos was not systematic by skin tone, and 0.62% of players with photos had missing height/weight data
an unreported sensitivity analysis found the height/weight exclusion had negligible impact
skin tone was averaged across the two raters and then dichotomized (light ≤0.25, dark ≥0.5)
red cards were converted into a binary indicator (any red card = 1)
rare positions were grouped into an 'Other' category
a logistic regression model (binary outcome) was fitted
the model formula was P(any_red_card) ~ dark_skin + games + position + league_country
estimation was performed via maximum likelihood
standard errors were clustered at the player level (1,372 clusters)
the player-level clustering approach is described as conservative and appropriate given the nested dyad-within-player structure
the risk difference was calculated via average marginal effects (counterfactual prediction method)
the standard error for the risk difference was obtained via the delta method
two-sided Wald tests at α=0.05 were used for inference
the dark_skin coefficient is β=0.104, SE=0.091, p=0.249
the games coefficient is β=0.130, SE=0.004, p<0.001, a strong positive effect
Center Backs have the highest position risk, β=1.06, p<0.001
France and Spain show higher red card rates than England (the reference league)
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by the analysis

spans.note: Lead-in to the evidence list supporting the conclusion

spans.assertion: the effect size is small: 0.125pp (1.22%→1.34%), about a 10% relative increase
the 95% CI (-0.088 to 0.337pp) includes zero, so the true effect could be negative, zero, or positive
p=0.249 is far above 0.05, providing insufficient evidence to reject the null
the observed difference is consistent with what would be expected from random sampling variation alone
the point estimate is positive (dark > light), so the direction is consistent with the hypothesis even though not significant
a sensitivity analysis using continuous skin tone found a statistically significant effect (p=0.040, OR=1.26 per unit)

spans.note: Speculative explanations: possible non-linearity, power loss from dichotomization, effects concentrated at extremes

spans.assertion: dark-skinned players represent only 18% of the sample
only 261 red cards occurred among dark-skinned player dyads
the analysis has limited statistical power to detect small effects
even if real, a 0.125pp difference is substantively very small in absolute/practical terms

spans.note: Observational data limitation: cannot establish causation, unmeasured confounding possible
Skin tone measurement limitations: photo-based, not standardized, rater influence, lighting/angle/quality, doesn't capture in-match referee perception

spans.note: Assumptions That Could Not Be Fully Met subheading

spans.assertion: dyads are not truly independent, being nested within players, referees, matches, and leagues
a multilevel model would have been more appropriate than the player-level clustering approach used
the analysis did not test for effect modification by referee country, league, position, or time period

spans.note: No unmeasured confounding is a strong assumption that cannot be verified with observational data

spans.assertion: a sensitivity analysis was run using the full continuous skin tone spectrum instead of dichotomizing
the continuous-measure analysis used N=123,868 dyads, including medium skin tones
the continuous-measure coefficient is β=0.229, SE=0.112, p=0.040
the odds ratio for very dark vs. very light skin is 1.26 (95% CI 1.01-1.57)
the continuous measure shows a statistically significant effect, suggesting a possible dose-response relationship or power loss from dichotomization
the sensitivity analysis suggests the hypothesis may have some support with a continuous measure, though the primary dichotomous comparison is not significant
